div.p: Too late to arrange. Y r card forwarded here. But he can simply apply to J. Cape. Hope all with you well.

div.note: The face of this postcard shows a photograph of “Feldkirch Neustadt,” a central street in Feldkirch, Austria, with the Hotel zum Loewen, where the Joyces were staying, visible on the left side of the street. The postcard was produced by L. Heim, a photo publisher in nearby Dornbirn. (For Feldkirch and JJ’s stay there, see note 2, below.)

Unidentified. The publisher Jonathan Cape, Ltd., of London, acquired from the Egoist Press in 1924 the rights to JJ’s Chamber Music, Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and Exiles. Herbert Jonathan Cape (1879-1960) founded the firm with Wren Howard in 1921, going on to publish works by H.G. Wells, W.H. Davies, Sinclair Lewis, Ernest Hemingway, Margaret Mead, and other authors. For additional details, see Nora Joyce to Pound, 22 February 1931, notes.

note.p: Feldkirch, a medieval town in western Austria, bordering on Switzerland and Liechtenstein. A contemporary guidebook described it as “an old town of 12,000 inhab., on the [River] Ill, … dominated by the [medieval castle] Schattenburg [with] a large Jesuit College. The parish church dates from the 15-16th centuries.” The Hotel zum Loewen (also spelled Löwen or Löwe) had “72 beds at 3½ to 8S” (Karl Baedeker, Austria Together with Budapest, Prague, Karlsbad, Marienbad, 12th rev. ed. [Leipzig: Karl Baedeker, 1929], 380).

In July 1932, JJ went to Zurich to consult his eye surgeon, Professor Alfred Vogt (1879-1943). He placed his daughter, Lucia(1907-1982), whose mental health was deteriorating, with a nurse under the supervision of friends, Eugène Jolas (1894-1952) and Maria Jolas (1893-1987), who were on family holiday in Feldkirch. After several weeks, JJ left Zurich for Feldkirch and stayed at the Hotel zum Loewen from 10 August to 6 September, in order to be with the restless, volatile Lucia, who worked on alphabet designs that were later used as decorated initial letters in A Chaucer A.B.C., published by The Obelisk Press of Paris with a preface by Louis Gillet in 1936. For a fuller account of Lucia’s alphabet designs, known as lettrines, see JJ to Pound, 9 November 1932, notes.
